To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
giant cell arteritis (GCA) can be detected by MRI in a high percentage of patients, with a high sensitivity and specificity.

(1) the presence of a large mural hyperintensity on the T2WI is highly predictive of GCA; (2) the absence of a mural hyperintensity excludes the diagnosis of GCA; and (3) mural hyperintensity is a dynamic sign that resolves with corticosteroid therapy.
the inflammatory activity of GCA is reflected by mural hyperenhancement (HE) in MRI, and that this activity can be assessed and followed over time by repeated MRI examinations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of a novel method for the detection of inflammatory processes in the human body.
the use of MRI to assess the presence and activity of GCA, and the effects of treatment with corticosteroids.
the study of atherosclerotic lesions in carotid arteries and their relationship with the presence and activity of GCA.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of an inflammatory mural hyperenhancement in the carotid arteries in giant cell arteritis (GCA) is not specific and that it is not possible to differentiate GCA from other forms of vasculitis based on the MRI findings alone.

MRI of the temporal arteries is a useful tool in the diagnosis of GCA and that the mural enhancement pattern in MRI is a reliable sign for GCA and can be used as an inclusion criterion for GCA in the ACR 1990 criteria for the diagnosis of GAA.
the presence of an intracranial aneurysm in patients with GCA is associated with a high risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage and that this risk can be reduced by early diagnosis and treatment of GCA.

there is a high prevalence of subclinical atherosclerosis in patients with giant cell arteritis, which is associated with a high risk of stroke.
